note: Quantitative analysis of war frequency, escalation and international order challenges simple decline narratives. Distinguishing war onset from severity offers reusable risk reasoning. Analytical argument rather than a statistics curriculum. Different tests add learning; causal identification and rare-event extrapolation remain uncertain. War central, T12 applies; broad modern-to-current argument has no single closed episode.

Pirate governance, incentives and credible commitments illustrate organization outside lawful enforcement. Distinct institutional arrangements add mechanisms rather than only colorful lives. Historical reconstructions and rational-choice interpretation merit less confidence than direct measurement; no high-confidence foundational veto established. Coercive governance/power central, T12 applies. Approximate golden-age endpoint 1730.

author: Robert C. Allen
note: Comparative development links wages, technology, institutions, trade and geography. Multiple regions test growth explanations; brevity alone is not the basis for density. Explanatory survey, not technical economics training. Production and development rather than finance or politics are central. Broad cross-period account, H13 zero.

author: Jeffrey G. Williamson
note: Comparative cases and econometric analysis connect specialization, commodity volatility, deindustrialization and income divergence. India, Turkey and Mexico supply different constraints. Quantitative evidence serves historical explanation, not a methods course. Trade and production central, neither thematic deduction. Approximate central nineteenth/early-twentieth-century endpoint 1950, low confidence.

State formation connects coercive capacity, capital concentration, extraction and cities across European cases. Different routes constrain a single war-making explanation; broad causal synthesis remains an interpretation rather than universal law. Dense comparisons are useful but conceptually demanding. Political and military power central, T12 applies. Revised named period ends 1992; original work 1990.

Ancient prices, trade, labor and institutions test market integration. Kenneth Harl supports the market interpretation but stresses that Roman price evidence cannot prove the strong integration claim; better Babylonian data offer a useful contrast. This substantial defense prevents treating contested details as an automatic V9 finding. Evidence attainment reduced for sparse identification. Main trade economy, not finance alone; no single modern nation. Approximate Roman-era endpoint 300 gives capped H13. First publisher release 2012, standard imprint 2013; year confidence moderate.

Chinese agrarian productivity, property, money, markets and state revenue are connected across long institutional change. Separate sectors add learning; an accessible economic history rather than technical training. China-centered narrative warrants T11. Main production and development, not finance alone, so T12 zero. Approximate nineteenth-century endpoint 1900.

Compares economic organization, social hierarchy, politics and religion across preindustrial societies. Shared constraints and contrasting cultures provide high transferable yield. Introductory social history is not technical training. Multiple eras and societies form a typological argument without one historical endpoint; politics and religion are integrated layers, not doctrinal truth assessment or the sole central domain. Original 1989 work, not 2015 reprint.

title: The Great Big Book of Horrible Things
note: Comparative atrocity chronicle collects death estimates with political and social context. Counts have uneven evidential foundations; no inference that rough rankings are precise measurements. Historical comparisons add some transferable constraints, so V3 is not established, despite large descriptive content and weak direct fit. War and political violence central, T12 applies. Broad cross-period coverage; original 2011 US publication, 2012 UK listing.

Disease history links pathogen evolution, settlement, mobility, institutions and prosperity across human history. Different epidemics and social settings add constraints; broad causal reconstruction is less certain than local evidence. Historical explanation, not health advice. Disease predominates, T11 applies; no single closed historical period.

title: China: A History
author: John Keay
note: Long national history connects dynasties, social institutions, invention and modern political change. Explanatory context supplies some transfer beyond names and dates; broad survey detail limits density and utility. China-centered political history triggers both thematic deductions. Whole-history survey crosses periods rather than one bounded episode. First work 2008; 2009 paperback is a reprint.

title: India: A History
author: John Keay
note: Separately nominated companion history, identified in Keay's publisher bibliography. Broad political, cultural and institutional synthesis offers some transferable context rather than only isolated events. India-centered politics warrants both thematic deductions. Density and content assessment rely on work identity and known scope, not inspected chapters; low confidence. Original 2000 date is also specified by the nominating source. No single central period.
Publisher specifies Grades 9 and up in a school/reference series. Primary precollege educational positioning triggers H5; adult readership or coverage depth does not override it.

Long history of Greek language, culture, institutions and diaspora connects ideas with their wider influence. Global connections prevent a purely local V3 verdict, though the central people's history warrants T11. Politics is one layer alongside cultural transmission, so T12 zero. Multiple civilizations and periods; no single endpoint deduction. Different periods add history rather than simple repetition.

Linguistics, archaeology and ancient DNA constrain competing homeland and migration accounts. History of changing evidence adds transferable inference lessons; not a language or excavation curriculum. Publisher certainty does not establish that the origin question is settled; assess interpretation cautiously. Broad history of research through current evidence, not only one prehistoric episode. No thematic deduction for analytical treatment of nationalist misuse.

author: Amanda H. Podany
note: Written records and archaeology reconstruct labor, commerce and institutions across the ancient Near East. Individual lives are windows onto systems, not isolated biographical detail; different social roles add learning. Multiple regions and production systems rather than one nation or politics alone. Explicit arc ends with Alexander's conquests, approximately 323 BCE; H13 capped.

author: Lester L. Grabbe
note: Source criticism and archaeology assess ancient Israel's history. Historical claims and evidence are central, not establishing the truth of religious doctrines; V8 does not follow from biblical material. Methods support a substantive narrative, not mainly technical proficiency. Contrasting source types add useful distinctions. One polity/cultural history warrants T11; approximate ancient endpoint yields capped H13.

Citizen-centered institutions, competition and economic development explain Greek prosperity and military outcomes. Comparative poleis add constraints; causal claims remain historical interpretations. Greek political development is central, so T11 and T12 apply. Classical-era endpoint approximately 323 BCE, H13 capped. Mechanistic narrative prevents V3 despite topic deductions.

Archaeology and ordinary working lives illuminate labor portfolios, consumption, saving and economic insecurity. Different occupations add constraints; illustrative individuals serve an economic account rather than personality narrative. Production and livelihoods are central, not finance alone. Roman imperial setting is transregional; no modern single-nation deduction. Approximate imperial endpoint 300 yields capped H13.

Nahuatl records support an Aztec history with indigenous institutions, conquest and adaptation. Historical use of neglected sources supplies transferable evidential lessons; not a minority-advocacy veto. Different phases add substantive history. Single civilization and political conquest central, both thematic deductions. Approximate early-colonial endpoint 1600 gives capped H13.

Indigenous texts and archaeology reconstruct Maya cultural and political history. Source methods and institutional context provide some transferable content, despite weak industrial fit. Different periods add historical knowledge. A single civilization predominates, T11 applies; culture as well as politics prevents T12 on the limited evidence. Approximate endpoint at the last independent Maya polity, 1697, low confidence; H13 capped regardless of plausible ancient/early-colonial endpoint.

State institutions, trade, landholding and wars explain Carthaginian development. Commercial organization provides transfer beyond battles; narrative is not a technical reference. A single polity with political/military arc central warrants both thematic deductions. Ends in destruction in 146 BCE, H13 capped. Diverse economic and social chapters add learning.

Medieval sexual life is explained through medical ideas, religious rules and lived practice. Historical social analysis is neither sexual-health advice nor assessment of doctrinal truth. Contrasts between prescriptions and behavior add learning; direct utility remains low. No single nation or named thematic category predominates. Approximate medieval endpoint 1500, H13 capped.
